articles.title: Grønland kutter i danskundervisning
articles.content:
De yngste grunnskoleelevene på Grønland får mindre danskundervisning i skolen, etter at ny opplæringslov ble vedtatt i nasjonalforsamlingen.

Det er elever fra 1. til 3. klasse som ikke lenger skal ha ordinær danskundervisning, skriver det danske nyhetsbyrået Ritzau med henvisning til Sermitsiaq.

Tidligere har danskundervisning vært obligatorisk på alle klassetrinn, men med den nye loven utsettes dette til 4. klasse.

I stedet får de yngste elevene dansk som et såkalt introduksjonsfag, i tillegg til færre fag og timer. Samtidig skal grønlandsk og matematikk prioriteres høyere.

– Målet er at elevene lærer de viktigste ferdighetene tidlig og samtidig får mer ro og trivsel på skolen, heter det i lovforslaget.

Grønland

                        The Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) has struggled with growing delays in processing skilled worker permits, and one main reason is Britons moving to Norway to work after Brexit.

At the end of October, the government proposed changes to the skilled worker permit rules after admitting the current system has serious problems that have put strain on resources and driven up waiting times.

To that end, the Ministry of Labour and Social Inclusion published a public consultation paper to gather feedback from social organisations and various stakeholders in Norway about the changes.

In its consultation document, the ministry explained that the main reasons for the proposal are that around 10 percent of cases have been identified as fraudulent, and that the system has been hit by bottlenecks and a big rise in applications for this type of permit across the country.

Authorities explicitly said that the number of applications has gone up sharply since 2021 after the United Kingdom left the EU and the European Economic Area (EEA).

Before Brexit, British citizens could simply register with the police using the fast-track EU/EEA scheme, avoiding the standard queue. However, since 2021, every British national hired in Norway must follow the longer and far more complex permit process used for non-EEA or third-country nationals. This represented a big chunk of new applications entering a system that was already stretched.

Data from UDI shows that just 124 work permits for British nationals, most in "other" categories instead of skilled or seasonal work, were granted in 2020, but the number then jumped to 1,321 in 2021, followed by 958 in 2022, 1,237 in 2023, and 950 in 2024.

The most recent figures show that a total of 1,095 British citizens received work permits as skilled workers, seasonal workers, or in other categories in 2025.

To put that into perspective, out of the 10,230 third-country nationals who got this type of permit last year, Brits made up 10.7 percent. That reflects the average extra workload the agency has handled from British applicants alone over the past five years.

– Kvar arbeidsplass har ulike risikoar knytt til arbeidet som bli utført. Desse må bli avdekt gjennom kartlegging og risikovurdering. Då kan verksemda finne gode tiltak som fjernar eller reduserer risikoen for at ulykker skjer. Det er arbeidsgjevars ansvar. Vi veit at dei fleste arbeidsulykker kunne vore unngått.

articles.content:

articles.content:

articles.content:

Bilen stanset ikke, og politiet fulgte etter i sydgående retning på E6 ved Karlshus.

Fem passasjerer løp fra bilen da den til slutt stoppet. Alle fem ble raskt innhentet av politipatruljer, opplyser politiet.

Flere politipatruljer, patruljehund, politiets innsatsleder og politihelikopter deltok i oppdraget.

Alle de involverte er under 18 år, og både barnevern og foresatte er varslet av politiet.

articles.content:
I Sør-Sudan er valget på nytt parlament og ny president utsatt fra desember til februar. Det får nyhetsbyrået Reuters bekreftet av landets valgkommisjon.

Valget – som allerede er blitt utsatt en gang – skulle etter planen funnet sted 22. desember. Den nye datoen blir 11. februar neste år.

Valgkommisjonen begrunner utsettelsen med at det trengs mer tid til forberedelsene.

I september uttalte FN-kommisjonen som overvåker og rapporterer om menneskerettighetene i Sør-Sudan at landet ikke var klar til å kunne gjennomføre et fritt og fredelige valg.

Valget blir det første siden landet ble selvstendig i 2011.

I 2013 førte en konflikt mellom president Salva Kiir og visepresident Riek Machar til en fem år lang borgerkrig.

Sør-Sudan

Sør-Sudan er preget av uro og konflikt på grunn av flere års borgerkrig. Ifølge FN forekommer det ofte seksuell vold, sult og brudd på menneskerettighetene i landet. I høst pågår det fredssamtaler mellom regjeringen og opprørsledere.

articles.content:

                        Transport chaos hits Oslo, Norwegian intelligence sees increased risk of Russian sabotage, budget partners struggle to reach an agreement on diesel taxes, and more news on Friday.

Air and rail transport have been severely disrupted in Oslo

First, heavy snowfall on Thursday affected more than 150 flights at Oslo Airport, mainly due to delays while crews cleared snow from the runways, public broadcaster NRK reported.

Monica Iren Fasting from airport operator Avinor told NRK that the cleanup work would continue through Thursday evening and into Friday night, so if you are travelling today, you should still expect some delays.

When it comes to trains, the problems also began on Thursday evening when a freight train derailed at Oslo Central Station (Oslo S). Authorities had to close part of the station after tracks 1 to 5 were blocked, causing delays and several cancellations.

However, the disruption continued into Friday morning when an electrical ground fault affected the station early in the day. Bane Nor, which manages the railway infrastructure, said it had to stop all traffic just after 6am and will give another update at 12pm.

Norwegian vocabulary: jordfeil - electrical ground fault

More than nine kroner per litre separates budget partners on diesel prices

Norwegian media report that a major disagreement over fuel taxes has come up in the national budget talks, as the Labour Party and its budget partners struggle to find common ground.

Within the negotiations, each party presents its alternative budget based on its priorities, and according to calculations by the newspaper Nationen, the Centre Party’s alternative budget would make diesel 4.51 kroner cheaper per litre by cutting CO₂ and road taxes, while the Green Party's proposal would raise diesel prices by 4.56 kroner per litre.

The Green Party says it would also set aside 15 billion kroner to compensate people for higher CO₂ taxes, which could represent over 20,000 kroner a year for a family of four living in a rural area. 
​
"It is simply an unrealistic and inhumane environmental policy that MDG is advocating when they want to increase taxes. It is completely out of the question for the Centre Party to let them get their way in the negotiations," said Centre Party deputy parliamentary leader Geir Pollestad, as reported by newspaper Aftenposten.
​
"MDG wants it to be worthwhile to choose climate-friendly options, while people in the rural areas get their money back through a climate bonus. Then most people will be left with more money", said MDG MP Frøya Sjursæther.
​
Other government budget partners also have different proposals. The Socialist Left Party (SV) wants to increase diesel prices by 1.68 kroner, while the Red Party  suggests a 79 øre cut (0.79 kroner).
​
Norwegian vocabulary: dieselprisen - the diesel price (this is one of the many compound words in Norwegian)

Norway intelligence sees increased risk of Russian sabotage

Norwegian intelligence on Thursday said there was an increased risk that Russia would carry out sabotage against targets in the Scandinavian country.

The Norwegian Police Security Service (PST) said in a statement that it had noted an uptick in the number of sabotage incidents in 2026, and that the security situation contributed "to increased risk-taking by Russian intelligence services".

"We believe there is good reason to expect that Russian intelligence will carry out sabotage in Norway in the coming year," said Inger Haugland, director of PST's department for state actors.

The agency said sabotage actions enlisted different methods but mentioned the discovery of a drone near a Ukrainian transport aircraft in Germany as a recent example, noting that German authorities had publicly suggested that Russia may be behind the incident.

In an updated threat assessment, PST said the most likely targets in Norway were "defence-related enterprises and companies that provide services to them" but critical infrastructure, such as the energy sector, could also be targeted.

Norwegian vocabulary: sabotasjetrussel - sabotage threat

READ THE FULL STORY: Norway intelligence sees increased risk of Russian sabotage

New national guide launched to tackle racism in Norwegian schools

Several recent analyses have shown that bullying and racism in schools are growing problems that many foreign families have to deal with in Norway.

To provide teachers, school leaders, and kindergarten staff with a new resource to help tackle the problem, the Centre for Equality KUN (Likestillingssenteret KUN) has launched a new online guide to recognise, prevent, and respond to racism in the classroom.

"All children have the right to a safe learning environment. Yet many experience that racism characterises everyday school life," said Viljar Eidsvik from KUN at the launch event.

The guide is free and offers practical methods and strategies for school staff based on findings from Save the Children organisation, which show that everyday prejudice, such as classroom exclusion or even comments about children's packed lunches, can affect students' wellbeing and learning.

"For children who are exposed to racism, it can have consequences for learning, health, and participation. Some withdraw from the community, refuse to participate in the classroom, or dread going to school," said Anne Elin Kleva from Save the Children.

Norwegian vocabulary: har rett til - have the right to

Norway will block Russian athletes from competing in the country

Norway's government said on Thursday that it would prevent Russian and Belarusian professional athletes from coming to Norway to compete, hours after neighbouring Finland announced a similar move.

It said that it intended to prevent athletes from these countries coming to Norway as long as the war in Ukraine continues.

Norway is preparing to host World Cup in cross-country skiing in December in the town of Trondheim, but this decision means that Russian and Belarusian athletes could be blocked from competing despite having been cleared by the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS).

The government noted in a statement that while Norway already had strict rules for visas for Russian and Belarusian citizens, recent "relaxations introduced by international sports federations" meant that more athletes and support staff from the two countries may come to the Scandinavian nation to compete.

To this end, the government said it would instruct immigration authorities and police "to refuse entry to Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and accompanying support staff... if they come to Norway to take part in sporting competitions".

Ytre høyrepartiet Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) har økt sin ledelse over Tysklands regjerende kristendemokrater og har nå en oppslutning på 28 prosent, ifølge en ny meningsmåling.

AfD får dermed 2 prosentpoeng høyere oppslutning enn i en tilsvarende måling for en uke siden.

Tysklands to kristendemokratiske partier CDU og CSU, som i fjor dannet regjering med sosialdemokratiske SDU, får en oppslutning på 22 prosent, 1 prosentpoeng mindre enn i den forrige målingen.

Hvis det hadde vært valg nå, ser det ikke ut til at de tre regjeringspartiene ville greid å sikre seg flertall i nasjonalforsamlingen.

Målingen ble fredag publisert av nyhetsbyrået DPA. Den ble utført 10.-12. november med 1297 tilfeldig utvalgte velgere. Feilmarginen er på mellom 2 og 3 prosentpoeng, og DPA understreker at meningsmålinger generelt er beheftet med usikkerhet.

Tyskland holder valg på ny nasjonalforsamling i begynnelsen av 2029, men det er foreløpig ikke fastsatt en nøyaktig valgdato. Forrige valg ble holdt i februar i fjor, og i mai samme år ble kristendemokraten Friedrich Merz forbundskansler.

articles.content:

                        Immigration and integration have been at the centre of a new row in Norway after a minister was forced to defend and explain her remarks that successive Norwegian governments had been too naive in the past.

Kjersti Stenseng, the Minister of Labour and Inclusion, sparked a row in Norway after stating on public broadcaster NRK's programme Debatten that "we have been too naive" regarding integration, pointing out that too many people are out of work, speak too little Norwegian, and live in areas with challenging living conditions.

Her comments triggered criticism from researcher and sociologist Astrid Ouahyb Sundsbø, who questioned in an opinion piece in NRK whether political rhetoric is part of the problem and if the system created by politicians leads to exclusion.

"If the government is serious about integration, they must stop with the simple rhetoric that immigrants are the problem, and start doing something about the obstacles inherent in the system they themselves have built," Sundsbø wrote, adding: "Placing the problem with refugees and immigrants not only simplifies politics, it also weakens the basis for solutions."

She further wrote that: "Naivety still remains in the understanding of the problem: Immigrants' language, culture and motivation are pointed out, as if the problem lies primarily with 'them' - and the responsibility for solving it too. A less naive understanding would have focused more on the systems we ourselves have built and the obstacles they create."

She even quoted a phrase that many in the international community can identify with: "Even with higher education, many remain stuck at the bottom."

In response, Stenseng explained that when she called Norway’s past approach "too naive," she was talking about politicians, not immigrants.

"When I acknowledge that we have been too naive, it is not a criticism of the people who have come here. We have underestimated how difficult it is to succeed with integration. And here, no party is exempt from criticism," she wrote in a follow-up column for NRK.

Stenseng admitted there have been problems in the past, but said that employment and education among people with immigrant backgrounds have improved over the last ten years.

"Compared to 2015, we see that more people who grow up in homes with parents with an immigrant background attend kindergarten and complete upper secondary education," Stenseng wrote.

"It shows a system that works. But that doesn't exempt us from talking about what doesn't work well enough. And that was also the point of entry into Debatten. It's not a criticism of the people who have come here."

The minister also said: "Integration is about both requirements and opportunities."

Drawing a sharp line against proposals from the right-wing Progress Party (FrP), she argued that slashing Norwegian language training and welfare support will not push newcomers into jobs faster.

"Integration succeeds when we as a society both stand up and make demands. This is also where the important difference between the Labour Party and the Progress Party lies. Some parties apparently believe that lower benefits and less support will solve the integration challenges," she wrote, warning that "demands without opportunities create exclusion."

She ended her column by saying the government will present a new national integration strategy in the spring, which will focus on workforce participation, living conditions, segregation, and cultural barriers that make integration harder.

articles.content:

                        After immigration authorities discovered cases of fraud in some skilled worker applications, Norway’s government announced planned changes to the system. What is actually happening, and when could the proposed new rules take effect?

At the end of October, Norway's Ministry of Labour and Social Inclusion published an initial proposal to update the rules for skilled worker residence permits by changing Chapter 6 of the Immigration Regulations (Utlendingsforskriften).

The Ministry suggested these changes after the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) found fraud in about 10 percent of non-EEA applications from foreign workers seeking to move to Norway.

READ MORE: What would Norway's planned changes to skilled worker visas mean for you?

According to the consultation paper, the reform aims to bring "amendments to Chapter 6 of the Immigration Regulations to counteract abuse of the labour immigration regulations and to facilitate faster and more resource-efficient case processing in the immigration administration."

This is especially relevant as the UDI also pointed out that dealing with fraud and investigating fake files has caused unusually long processing times.

The proposal includes tougher requirements and wider grounds for rejection, required electronic checks for employers to prevent false job offers, some relief for graduates and job seekers, permission for skilled workers to have a second job, and updates for self-employed.

These recent announcements have made some applicants worried about what happens next, especially those planning to move to Norway in the near future or renew their visas. At the same time, foreign residents already living in Norway under the skilled worker rules may feel more at ease as it may provide them more opportunities financially and for the development of their career.

It’s important to understand that this reform is not  going to be a new law, so it does not need to go through parliament or require debates and a formal vote in the Storting.

Instead, it involves regulatory amendments to secondary legislation, and as these are changes to the Immigration Regulations, the government can put them in place via regulatory decree.

This means that the Ministry of Labour and Social Inclusion, which is leading the proposal, and the executive branch manage the process internally, allowing it to move faster than a normal new bill or major legal change.

The current phase of this process is an open public consultation (høring) that will run for three months until January 22nd, 2027.

The Ministry has asked many organisations and groups to give their expert opinions. These include social organisations that work with immigrants (such as Caritas Norway, the MiRA Resource Centre for Black, Immigrant and Refugee Women, the Norwegian Red Cross, and Save the Children), state agencies such as the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV) and the Directorate for Integration and Diversity (IMDi), trade unions like the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO), and universities and educational institutions such as OsloMet, the University of Oslo (UiO), and NTNU, among many others.

However, the consultation is also open to the general public. This means that anyone may submit formal feedback on the proposed tightening of residency requirements. You can submit your input directly on the government's website.

After the public consultation closes in January, the Ministry will review and analyse all feedback. Based on this input, authorities will either adjust the draft or proceed as it is.

Once the Ministry finishes the final version, it will be formally adopted by the government. That’s when the changes will officially take effect.

Nevertheless, the ministry might also present the final rules to the King-in-Council (Kongen i statsråd in Norwegian), which is the weekly cabinet between the prime minister, other ministers and King Haakon, before the changes take effect.

There is no way of knowing exactly when the proposal will take effect, but given the process described above, it indicates that the changes may come into force in summer 2027, or possibly a little earlier if the government makes it a priority.

Since the proposed package has stricter rules for new applicants but also some possible benefits for foreigners already living in Norway, people feel a mix of worry, relief, and uncertainty about what’s coming.

However, the final measures and exact changes will not be known until the entire process has been completed or the government shares them beforehand.

One thing that is expected, however, is that if approved, the measures would be implemented directly by the UDI, which, based on what the government has said, should also speed up application processing times.

articles.title: FN-sjefen refser inntektsboom i oljebransjen: – Moralsk uakseptabelt
articles.content:
Rekordinntekter fører til at FN-sjef, Antonio Guterres, krever at lands regjeringer setter befolkningene sine foran penger.

– Regjeringene er nødt til å beskytte interessene til sitt folk – ikke interessene til en gruppe selskap, sier FN-sjefen til nyhetsbyrået AFP i forbindelse med klimatoppmøtet COP31 i Antalya i Tyrkia.

Han omtaler det som «absurd» og «moralsk uakseptabelt» at ni store fossilenergigiganter er ventet å håve inn til sammen 95 milliarder dollar i inntekter i løpet av ett enkelt kvartal samtidig som vanlige folk sliter med å ha råd til oppvarming og drivstoff.

Han er også kritisk til nye prosjekter rettet mot fossil energi.

– Det gir ingen mening å sette i gang nye prosjekter innen fossil energi, sier 77-åringen og legger til:

– Jeg skulle åpenbart helst sett at landene som deltar på dette klimatoppmøtet hadde satte synspunkt, inkludert arrangørene.

Klima og miljø

Verden opplever allerede klimaendringene, slår FNs klimapanel fast. Mer ekstremvær, høyere havnivå og økte helseproblemer er noen av konsekvensene, ifølge deres siste hovedrapport.

Oljeprisen

Prisen på nordsjøolje kan svinge kraftig, og påvirkes blant annet av kriger og konflikter i verden.

                        Heavy snowfall causes traffic accidents and chaos across Norway, the Minister of Labour and Inclusion defends her integration remarks by insisting "immigrants are not the problem", and more news on Thursday.

Snow hits Norway, causing road chaos and public transport disruptions

On Tuesday, meteorologists warned that snow was on its way to Norway, with up to 15 centimetres expected in Eastern Norway and up to 30 centimetres in the north.

At first, the snowfall in easter Norway was forecast for Oslo, Akershus, Østfold, Vestfold, and lower Buskerud. However, on Thursday morning, the warning was extended to more areas, and a yellow danger alert now includes Innlandet and Hamar.

A separate snow warning was also issued on Wednesday for parts of Western Norway.

As is often the case, the first heavy snowfall of the season has caused problems across the country. Public transport services have been cancelled, and there have been many road accidents, including several vehicles sliding off slippery roads. For example, a school bus slid off the road in Larvik.

"We are receiving a number of reports of skids, traffic accidents and slippery driving conditions in connection with the recent snowfall," operations manager Per Magne Eftang, from the South-East Police District, wrote in the police log just before 8am, according to daily Aftenposten.

"The snowfall causes changed driving conditions, which in turn change road grip and braking distances. Plan to spend a little longer than usual getting to work and appointments. Drive according to the conditions and keep a good distance from the vehicle in front," he added.

If there was any lingering doubt, you should already have winter tyres fitted if you are driving.

She ended her column by saying the government will present a new national integration strategy in the spring that will focus on workforce participation, living conditions, segregation, and cultural barriers that make integration harder.

Human rights groups criticise Norway over handling of torture survivors in asylum system

A group of human rights organisations has sent a report to the UN Committee against torture, warning that Norway still does not meet its international obligations for asylum seekers and immigration detainees.

The report says that several problems raised in earlier UN reviews still have not been fixed, and that Norway still does not have a required system to identify torture victims among asylum seekers, putting vulnerable people at risk of having their claims wrongly rejected.

The report also criticises the state's five-hour cap on legal aid in standard asylum cases as insufficient when interpreters are needed, alongside concerns over the care of unaccompanied minor asylum seekers, and raises concerns about conditions at the Trandum immigration detention centre.

Jon Ole Martinsen, senior adviser at the Norwegian Organisation for Asylum Seekers (NOAS), told multicultural newspaper Utrop regarding the findings that: "We think it is high time that political decision-makers now initiate the necessary measures to rectify these conditions. It should be absolutely central for Norwegian politicians that we are well within the obligations we have under the Torture Convention."

"We hope that the report will help raise the issues and hopefully eventually lead to changes in practice, and not just political speeches about how important international conventions are and how important it is for Norway to follow them," he added

A cyberattack on software provider Front Systems, which is used by more than 10 percent of clothing stores in Norway, has exposed customer and employee data, according to business daily E24.

The breach happened on November 5th and attackers had access for four hours to the system, giving them time to take about 0.2 percent of the database, including customer names, email addresses and employee login details.

Fortunately, credit card details were not compromised, since payment card data is not stored in the system.

PM Støre falls ill, forced to cancel planned trip to Dublin

At this time of year, many people are getting seasonal illnesses, and Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre is no exception.

On Thursday, Støre was supposed to travel to Dublin to attend the European Political Community (EPC) summit with leaders from about 50 countries, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

However, Norwegian newspaper Aftenposten reported that Støre had to cut his plans short and is already flying back home.

                        Snow has arrived across large parts of Norway, bringing a bit of chaos to the cities: from public transport disruptions to damaged cars on the roads and many people unable to reach their destinations.

On Tuesday, meteorologists warned that winter snow was on its way to Norway, with up to 15 centimetres expected in Eastern Norway and up to 30 centimetres in the north.

The snowfall was initially forecast across Oslo, Akershus, Østfold, Vestfold, and lower parts of Buskerud. However, on Thursday morning, the warning was extended to cover several additional areas, with a yellow danger alert now in place for Innlandet and Hamar.

A separate snow warning was also issued on Wednesday for parts of Western Norway.

As is often the case, the first heavy snowfall of the season has caused problems across the country. Public transport services have been cancelled, and there have been many road accidents, including several vehicles sliding off slippery roads.

"It's always surprising how little snow it takes to cause problems. There's always chaos with the first snowfall," said meteorologist Hanne Beate Skattør at the Norwegian Meteorological Institute as reported by newspaper Aftenposten.

"We are receiving a number of reports of skids, traffic accidents and slippery driving conditions in connection with the recent snowfall," operations manager Per Magne Eftang, from the South-East Police District, wrote in the police log just before 8am, according to another article from the daily.

"The snowfall causes changed driving conditions, which in turn change road grip and braking distances. Plan to spend a little longer than usual getting to work and appointments. Drive according to the conditions and keep a good distance from the vehicle in front," he added.

If there was any lingering doubt, you should already have winter tyres fitted if you are driving.

Some of the most notable incidents include dozens of buses cancelled in Vestfold and a school bus sliding off the road in Larvik. "The bus has skidded off the road and into the ditch with all four wheels. There are 24 children on the bus who appear unharmed,"   the police log said, according to public broadcaster NRK.

READ MORE: What you need to know about winter driving in Norway

With the first snowflakes falling in Oslo at 5.30am, public transport delays and traffic disruptions also hit the capital.

According to newspaper VG, over 1,000 bus departures were delayed and 65 percent of bus routes in the area were cancelled.

Oslo police also received several reports of fallen trees damaging parked cars. On the E6 motorway at Skulleruddumpa, two lorries became stuck. "One is facing out of Oslo and the other is facing into Oslo. This is causing some traffic problems at the scene," police reported.

The snowy weather also affected Oslo Airport, causing several delays, although staff from airport operator Avinor said they were working hard to clear the runways.

"There has been a lot of snow at Oslo Airport, so it is in full winter operation. We are ploughing continuously. It is quite normal under such conditions that there will also be some delays in air traffic. All the planes also have to go through de-icing before they can take off," communications adviser Helena W. Jensen at Avinor told NRK.
